title: 10th Grade Language Arts
subtitle: English II · 36-Week Comprehensive Course

units.title: Foundations of Scholarly Reading & Writing
units.essential: How do disciplined readers and writers build trustworthy interpretations?
units.summary: Establish scholar habits, diagnostic baselines, annotation, inference, paraphrase, summary, academic integrity, and assessment readiness.
units.assessment: Diagnostic portfolio: annotated reading, analytical paragraph, revised writing sample, and reflection.

units.title: Coming-of-Age & Literary Layers
units.essential: How do authors use character, conflict, setting, and perspective to create layered meaning?
units.summary: Analyze literary elements, coming-of-age experiences, conflicts, point of view, and competing perspectives.
units.assessment: Character and perspective analysis with evidence map and discussion reflection.

units.title: Theme, Voice & Literary Analysis
units.essential: How do theme, diction, syntax, voice, and revision shape a literary interpretation?
units.summary: Compare universal themes, examine author style, and complete a formal literary analysis essay through drafting and revision.
units.assessment: Multi-paragraph literary analysis essay and revision memo.

units.title: American Speeches, Essays & Rhetoric
units.essential: How do historical writers shape central ideas and persuade particular audiences?
units.summary: Study historical American speeches and essays for structure, central idea, purpose, audience, appeals, devices, and rhetorical effectiveness.
units.assessment: Rhetorical analysis essay on a historical American speech or essay.

units.title: Argument, Debate & Civic Discourse
units.essential: How can a writer or speaker argue responsibly, fairly, and persuasively?
units.summary: Compare opposing arguments, evaluate validity, write claims and counterclaims, and participate in structured discussion and debate.
units.assessment: Evidence-based argument essay with oral defense or formal debate.

units.title: Synthesis & Midyear Mastery
units.essential: How do readers synthesize sources and use feedback to demonstrate midyear mastery?
units.summary: Synthesize information, refine grammar and style, organize portfolio evidence, and complete the cumulative midterm.
units.assessment: Source synthesis project, writing portfolio conference, and cumulative midterm examination.

units.title: Poetry, Ambiguity & Sound
units.essential: How do poets create layered meaning through speaker, image, sound, form, and ambiguity?
units.summary: Analyze poetic speaker, ambiguity, connotation, figurative language, mood, structure, sound, and comparison.
units.assessment: Comparative poetry analysis essay and expressive reading.

units.title: Classical, Mythic & Religious Adaptation
units.essential: What changes—and what remains—when foundational stories are adapted across time, culture, genre, or medium?
units.summary: Read mythical, classical, and religious source texts as literature, then compare adaptations across texts and media.
units.assessment: Comparative adaptation essay or multimedia analysis.

units.title: Research Foundations
units.essential: How do researchers ask focused questions and build reliable, ethical source records?
units.summary: Design research questions, evaluate reliability and bias, take accurate notes, paraphrase, cite, and synthesize.
units.assessment: Research proposal, annotated bibliography, source evaluation matrix, and synthesis paragraph.

units.title: Research Writing & Digital Publication
units.essential: How do writers transform research into clear, ethical, audience-ready publications?
units.summary: Write expository and argumentative research products, integrate sources, revise, publish digitally, and present findings.
units.assessment: Research paper, publication-ready digital product, and formal presentation.

units.title: Drama, Shakespeare & Performance
units.essential: How does performance reveal conflict, irony, rhetoric, and character more fully than silent reading alone?
units.summary: Study dramatic structure, stagecraft, irony, Shakespearean language, rhetoric, interpretation, and performance.
units.assessment: Dramatic analysis and staged or recorded performance with reflection.

units.title: Novel Study, Final Portfolio & Examination
units.essential: What evidence best demonstrates mature reading, writing, research, speaking, and reflection?
units.summary: Complete a long-form novel study, synthesize themes and perspectives, curate the final portfolio, and complete the final examination.
units.assessment: Novel analysis, student-led portfolio conference, cumulative final examination, and completion certificate.

quiz.question: What is the biggest academic shift from 9th to 10th grade ELA?
choices: Writing shorter answers
Analyzing deeper layers of meaning, ambiguity, rhetoric, and conflicting perspectives
Avoiding difficult texts
Only memorizing vocabulary
quiz.explanation: Grade 10 emphasizes deeper analysis, comparison, rhetoric, synthesis, and readiness for high-stakes ELA assessment.

quiz.question: What should students preserve for a portfolio?
choices: Only books they disliked
Only quiz scores
Reading/activity logs, writing samples, drafts, feedback, revisions, and reflections

quiz.question: Which action best demonstrates mastery of Week 01: Course Launch, Diagnostic & Scholar Habits?

Focus on page appearance while ignoring meaning
establish a baseline, organize course materials, and explain evidence-based reasoning
Summarize the topic without evidence or explanation

quiz.question: In ENGLISH-10 Week 01 (Course Launch, Diagnostic & Scholar Habits), a learner is studying diagnostic. Two sources about the same question differ in their conclusions. How should a research writer proceed?
choices: Select the longer source because page count indicates reliability.
Average the two conclusions without examining what each measured.
Omit the conflicting source to make the paragraph appear consistent.
Check provenance and methods, compare relevant evidence, and explain any remaining disagreement in the synthesis.
quiz.explanation: Research synthesis evaluates evidence and records disagreement rather than hiding it.

quiz.question: For Week 01 (Course Launch, Diagnostic & Scholar Habits), the language focus includes sentence boundaries, paragraph unity, and complete thoughts. Which sentence pair corrects a comma splice and preserves the meaning?
choices: After comparing the two accounts. Revised her conclusion.
The writer compared two accounts. She then revised her conclusion.
The writer compared two accounts, she then revised her conclusion.
The writer compared two accounts she then revised her conclusion.
quiz.explanation: Two complete independent clauses require correct separation or joining.

lessons.objective: Frame the week’s focus—Course Launch, Diagnostic & Scholar Habits—and build the vocabulary and background knowledge needed for independent work.

lessons.title: Close Reading & Evidence Lab
lessons.objective: Apply close-reading routines to establish a baseline, organize course materials, and explain evidence-based reasoning.

lessons.title: Composition & Craft Studio
lessons.objective: Transform reading and discussion evidence into diagnostic analytical response and individual grade 10 literacy growth plan.

lessons.title: Discussion, Feedback & Revision
lessons.objective: Use collaborative reasoning and targeted revision to improve clarity, accuracy, audience fit, and intellectual fairness.

lessons.title: Mastery Check, Corrections & Portfolio

choices: Add unsupported opinions
Remove the main idea
Keep the source’s meaning but use original wording
Change one word and keep the rest

quiz.question: A valid interpretation usually needs...
choices: Only one quote
Only a summary
No evidence
A claim, evidence, and explanation of how the evidence supports the claim
quiz.explanation: Evidence must be interpreted through reasoning.

quiz.question: Which action best demonstrates mastery of Week 02: Close Reading, Annotation & Inference?
choices: annotate purposeful details, distinguish observation from inference, and explain significance
Summarize the topic without evidence or explanation

Focus on page appearance while ignoring meaning

quiz.question: In ENGLISH-10 Week 02 (Close Reading, Annotation & Inference), a learner is studying annotation. Two passages appear to share a theme. Which interpretation shows careful close reading?

Use a summary of one passage as complete evidence for both.
Use a detail from each passage, explain the differing author choices, and qualify the common theme.
Identify the topic and call it a theme without considering either text.
quiz.explanation: Themes emerge from analyzed textual details and context, not a topic label alone.

quiz.question: For Week 02 (Close Reading, Annotation & Inference), the language focus includes phrases, clauses, sentence patterns, and precise evidence integration. Which analytical sentence integrates evidence and reasoning responsibly?

The account proves everyone agreed, even though other views were not recorded.
Because a detail appears in print, it needs no contextual examination.
The writer can omit conflicting evidence to keep the argument simple.
quiz.explanation: Clear analysis distinguishes recorded observation, plausible inference, and unresolved uncertainty.

choices: What words, structures, or details create this effect?
How many pages are there?
Do I like this text?
Can I skip the hard paragraph?

choices: Avoiding discussion
Rereading, annotating, summarizing, and questioning
Skipping unknown words
Reading only the title
quiz.explanation: Complex texts reward active strategies.

quiz.question: In ENGLISH-10 Week 03 (Paraphrase, Summary, Academic Integrity & FAST Baseline), a learner is studying paraphrase. A student makes a confident claim about the week's text. Which next step demonstrates transferable analytical reasoning?
choices: Discard any detail that complicates the preferred conclusion.
Locate specific evidence, explain the inference step, and name one reasonable limitation or alternative.
Repeat the claim more forcefully without adding evidence.
Replace interpretation with a list of isolated quotations.
quiz.explanation: Sound interpretation requires evidence, explanation, and acknowledgement of scope.

quiz.question: For Week 03 (Paraphrase, Summary, Academic Integrity & FAST Baseline), the language focus includes quotation marks, attribution phrases, pronoun reference, and concise summary. Which sentence distinguishes sourced words from analysis?
choices: The report proves everything; no attribution is needed.
A close synonym makes a copied sentence independent writing.
Quotation marks are unnecessary if the borrowed phrase is short.
The report uses the phrase “limited sample”; the writer then explains how that constraint narrows the conclusion and records the citation.
quiz.explanation: Quoted language and borrowed ideas must be credited and analytically distinguished.

lessons.miniLesson: Introduce the essential question. Model how a Grade 10 scholar previews a task, names the target skill, activates relevant context, and records precise academic vocabulary: synthesis, connection, pattern, source role, coherence.
lessons.guidedPractice: Preview the week’s text/source family: Three short sources offering complementary information on one topic. Complete a notice–wonder–predict routine and identify where standards ELA.10.C.1.4, ELA.10.C.4.1, ELA.10.R.3.2 will appear in the work.
lessons.independentWork: Create a five-term vocabulary record with definition, context sentence, connotation or word-part note, and an original application. Write an initial 6–8 sentence response to: “How do writers combine multiple sources into one coherent explanation?”
lessons.evidence: Vocabulary record, source preview notes, and initial response
lessons.support: Use sentence frames, a vocabulary bank, audio reading, chunked text, or teacher-selected background resources as needed.
lessons.extension: Locate a second text or real-world example that complicates the essential question and explain the connection.

lessons.title: Close Reading & Evidence Lab
lessons.objective: Apply close-reading routines to organize sources by ideas and relationships rather than summarizing one at a time.
lessons.miniLesson: Model a two-pass reading: first for comprehension and structure, then for evidence, author choices, patterns, contradictions, and significance. Review the difference between quotation, paraphrase, inference, and commentary.
lessons.guidedPractice: Read or reread the assigned selection. Annotate at least eight purposeful details and classify each annotation by skill or standard. Use the week’s language focus—source integration, varied attribution, transitions, and paragraph coherence—when writing notes.
lessons.independentWork: Complete an evidence ladder: observation → quotation/detail → paraphrase → inference → reasoning → significance. Identify the strongest and weakest evidence and justify the ranking.
lessons.evidence: Annotated text, evidence ladder, and one defensible inference
lessons.support: Reduce the text span, provide guided annotation symbols, pre-highlight one model passage, or allow oral rehearsal before writing.
lessons.extension: Develop a plausible alternative interpretation and identify the evidence that would support or weaken it.

lessons.title: Composition & Craft Studio
lessons.objective: Transform reading and discussion evidence into synthesis matrix and multi-source expository response.
lessons.miniLesson: Analyze a mentor paragraph or product for controlling idea, organization, integrated evidence, commentary, transitions, voice, and the week’s language focus: source integration, varied attribution, transitions, and paragraph coherence.
lessons.guidedPractice: Plan the product with a claim or controlling idea, evidence sequence, reasoning notes, and audience/purpose check. Draft one section collaboratively or through teacher modeling.
lessons.independentWork: Draft the week’s major product: Synthesis matrix and multi-source expository response. Highlight the sentence with the strongest reasoning and mark one place that still needs development.
lessons.evidence: Plan, draft, and self-identified revision target
lessons.support: Use an outline, paragraph frame, speech-to-text, model sentence patterns, or reduced writing length while maintaining the same thinking target.
lessons.extension: Revise one paragraph twice for two different audiences or tones and explain the consequences of each revision.

lessons.title: Discussion, Feedback & Revision
lessons.objective: Use collaborative reasoning and targeted revision to improve clarity, accuracy, audience fit, and intellectual fairness.
lessons.miniLesson: Practice the feedback protocol: affirm a strength, ask a genuine question, identify one evidence or reasoning gap, and recommend one precise revision. Review active listening, paraphrasing a peer, and respectful disagreement.
lessons.guidedPractice: Discuss the essential question using at least two pieces of evidence. Compare interpretations or approaches, then test each against the text, source quality, or task criteria.
lessons.independentWork: Revise the Wednesday product. Complete a revision memo naming at least three changes, the reason for each change, and the effect on the reader or listener.
lessons.evidence: Discussion record, peer/teacher feedback, revised product, and revision memo
lessons.support: Allow written discussion, partner rehearsal, teacher conference, checklist-based feedback, or one focused revision target.
lessons.extension: Write a brief response to the strongest counterinterpretation or counterargument raised during discussion.

lessons.title: Mastery Check, Corrections & Portfolio

lessons.miniLesson: Review the week’s vocabulary, standards language, and one common misconception. Model how to correct an error by naming the skill, explaining the mistake, and showing the corrected reasoning.

The writer compared two accounts she then revised her conclusion.

choices: Present the earlier draft, a substantial revision, and an explanation of changes tied to feedback or new evidence.
Present only the polished final copy and claim improvement is self-evident.
Use the total page count as the main proof of learning.
Remove all recorded mistakes so the process appears flawless.
quiz.explanation: Authentic learning evidence includes process, justification, and preserved revision history.

quiz.question: For Week 36 (Final Review, Final Examination & Completion), the language focus includes cumulative conventions, editing, vocabulary, and evidence integration. Which sentence pair corrects a comma splice and preserves the meaning?
choices: The writer compared two accounts she then revised her conclusion.
After comparing the two accounts. Revised her conclusion.
The writer compared two accounts. She then revised her conclusion.
The writer compared two accounts, she then revised her conclusion.
quiz.explanation: Two complete independent clauses require correct separation or joining.

lessons.title: Launch, Context & Vocabulary
lessons.objective: Frame the week’s focus—Final Review, Final Examination & Completion—and build the vocabulary and background knowledge needed for independent work.
lessons.miniLesson: Introduce the essential question. Model how a Grade 10 scholar previews a task, names the target skill, activates relevant context, and records precise academic vocabulary: transfer, mastery, correction, reflection, completion.
lessons.guidedPractice: Preview the week’s text/source family: Cumulative unfamiliar passages, course portfolio, and year-end review materials. Complete a notice–wonder–predict routine and identify where standards ELA.10.R.1.1, ELA.10.R.2.4, ELA.10.R.3.4 will appear in the work.
lessons.independentWork: Create a five-term vocabulary record with definition, context sentence, connotation or word-part note, and an original application. Write an initial 6–8 sentence response to: “How can I demonstrate transfer, correct misunderstandings, and plan for English III?”
lessons.evidence: Vocabulary record, source preview notes, and initial response
lessons.support: Use sentence frames, a vocabulary bank, audio reading, chunked text, or teacher-selected background resources as needed.
lessons.extension: Locate a second text or real-world example that complicates the essential question and explain the connection.

lessons.title: Close Reading & Evidence Lab
lessons.objective: Apply close-reading routines to apply course skills independently, analyze errors, and document readiness for the next course.
lessons.miniLesson: Model a two-pass reading: first for comprehension and structure, then for evidence, author choices, patterns, contradictions, and significance. Review the difference between quotation, paraphrase, inference, and commentary.
lessons.guidedPractice: Read or reread the assigned selection. Annotate at least eight purposeful details and classify each annotation by skill or standard. Use the week’s language focus—cumulative conventions, editing, vocabulary, and evidence integration—when writing notes.
lessons.independentWork: Complete an evidence ladder: observation → quotation/detail → paraphrase → inference → reasoning → significance. Identify the strongest and weakest evidence and justify the ranking.
lessons.evidence: Annotated text, evidence ladder, and one defensible inference
lessons.support: Reduce the text span, provide guided annotation symbols, pre-highlight one model passage, or allow oral rehearsal before writing.
lessons.extension: Develop a plausible alternative interpretation and identify the evidence that would support or weaken it.

lessons.title: Composition & Craft Studio
lessons.objective: Transform reading and discussion evidence into cumulative final examination, corrections, final reflection, and certificate record.
lessons.miniLesson: Analyze a mentor paragraph or product for controlling idea, organization, integrated evidence, commentary, transitions, voice, and the week’s language focus: cumulative conventions, editing, vocabulary, and evidence integration.
lessons.guidedPractice: Plan the product with a claim or controlling idea, evidence sequence, reasoning notes, and audience/purpose check. Draft one section collaboratively or through teacher modeling.
lessons.independentWork: Draft the week’s major product: Cumulative final examination, corrections, final reflection, and certificate record. Highlight the sentence with the strongest reasoning and mark one place that still needs development.
lessons.evidence: Plan, draft, and self-identified revision target
lessons.support: Use an outline, paragraph frame, speech-to-text, model sentence patterns, or reduced writing length while maintaining the same thinking target.
lessons.extension: Revise one paragraph twice for two different audiences or tones and explain the consequences of each revision.

lessons.title: Discussion, Feedback & Revision
lessons.objective: Use collaborative reasoning and targeted revision to improve clarity, accuracy, audience fit, and intellectual fairness.
lessons.miniLesson: Practice the feedback protocol: affirm a strength, ask a genuine question, identify one evidence or reasoning gap, and recommend one precise revision. Review active listening, paraphrasing a peer, and respectful disagreement.
lessons.guidedPractice: Discuss the essential question using at least two pieces of evidence. Compare interpretations or approaches, then test each against the text, source quality, or task criteria.
lessons.independentWork: Revise the Wednesday product. Complete a revision memo naming at least three changes, the reason for each change, and the effect on the reader or listener.
lessons.evidence: Discussion record, peer/teacher feedback, revised product, and revision memo
lessons.support: Allow written discussion, partner rehearsal, teacher conference, checklist-based feedback, or one focused revision target.
lessons.extension: Write a brief response to the strongest counterinterpretation or counterargument raised during discussion.

lessons.title: Mastery Check, Corrections & Portfolio
lessons.objective: Demonstrate weekly mastery and determine whether to advance, revise, or repeat targeted practice.
lessons.miniLesson: Review the week’s vocabulary, standards language, and one common misconception. Model how to correct an error by naming the skill, explaining the mistake, and showing the corrected reasoning.
lessons.guidedPractice: Complete a short retrieval warm-up, compare answers with notes, and identify one skill that needs deliberate attention before the quiz.
lessons.independentWork: Take the weekly quiz. Complete corrections for missed items. File the strongest artifact in the portfolio and write a 3–4 sentence reflection connecting evidence of growth to the essential question.
lessons.evidence: Quiz score, corrections, portfolio artifact, and reflection
lessons.support: Permit extended time, read-aloud where appropriate, reduced visual load, or a second attempt after corrections.
lessons.extension: Create one original quiz question with four choices, a definitive answer, and an explanation.
